title: kv-cache-reuse-eviction-paging-memory-bandwidth-investigation-2026-03-22
content:
Summary:

This note summarizes a set of profiling experiments and microbenchmarks focused on KV cache management in the serving runtime. Primary goals: measure effective KV reuse rates across realistic workloads, quantify eviction and paging costs, and understand the sensitivity of throughput/latency to GPU memory bandwidth and host<->device transfer patterns.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We rely on an in-memory KV cache to avoid re-computing key/value projections for prefix tokens. For long-context or multi-turn chat workloads the cache can dominate memory and bandwidth.
- Observed variability in tail latency and token throughput under heavy multi-session workloads. Hypothesis: suboptimal reuse patterns + eviction/paging overheads are contributing to increased per-token latency and reduced throughput.

Concrete questions:
1) What is the end-to-end cost (time + PCIe/NVLink traffic) of a cache miss vs a cache hit at typical sequence length distributions and batch sizes?
2) How often are cached entries reused (reuse rate) under representative traffic (chat, instruction, short prompts)?
3) How much does eviction policy choice (LRU / segmented LRU / clock) affect reuse and I/O?
4) When memory pressure forces paging (host<->device), how much does bandwidth limit throughput on our supported hardware (A100 40GB, A100 80GB, H100 in 80GB config)?
5) Are there identifiable hotspots for memcpy/device-to-device that could be optimized (kernel fusion, pinned memory pools)?

Methodology / experimental setup:
- Code: local perf harness in serving-runtime branch profiling/kv-cache-experiments (PR reference in linked_artifacts). Microbenchmarks added to run a configurable mix of sessions, sequence length distributions, and token step rates.
- Models: llama-2-13b (fp16); quantized 4bit model variant used for capacity tests. Use same attention+KV projection sizes as model on mainline.
- Hardware: experiments run on: A100-80GB (pinned server), H100-80GB (dev cluster), and an A100-40GB with NVLink off (representative of smaller instance).
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces:
  * chat_multi_turn: 10k sessions, avg prefix 120 tokens, median response 64 tokens, interleaved requests simulating web socket streaming.
  * short_prompts: many 1-2 turn requests, avg prefix 12 tokens, high QPS.
  * long_context: single-session long prefix 2048 tokens, to stress memory and eviction.
- Metrics captured:
  * reuse_rate = reused_kv_token_count / total_requested_kv_token_count (per-request and aggregated)
  * evictions_per_minute (per-device)
  * host_device_bw (GB/s), device_device_bw (GB/s)
  * per_token_latency P50/P95/P99
  * throughput (tokens/s)
  * kernel-level timeline trace (NVIDIA Nsight or CUPTI traces) for device memcpy and kernel launches
- Profiling tools: CUPTI traces, Nsight systems, nvprof for microbenchmarks, perf for CPU-side measurements, and custom counters instrumented in the runtime.

Baseline observations:
- Under chat_multi_turn on A100-80GB with KV cache sized to hold ~80% of active prefixes, reuse_rate ~72% aggregate, P95 per-token latency ~42ms, throughput ~1100 tokens/s. Host<->device transfers observed 5-8GB/s sustained during bursts (peak short windows 14GB/s).
- short_prompts workload shows lower reuse_rate (~18%) because many requests have unique small prefixes. Eviction churn high: evictions_per_minute ~2200, leading to frequent host<->device writes (paging). P95 token latency ~18ms but tail (P99) spikes when eviction+page-in coincides with request.
- long_context: reuse_rate ~95% (single session), but memory pressure forced paging on A100-40GB; observed device<->host bandwidth saturating at ~22GB/s and token throughput dropping to ~600 tokens/s.

Eviction policy comparison (small microbenchmarks):
- Policies tested: naive LRU (linked list), clock approximation, segmented LRU (hot/cold) with admission window.
- For chat_multi_turn: segmented LRU improved reuse_rate modestly (+3-5 percentage points) and reduced evictions_per_minute by ~18% vs naive LRU. Tail latencies (P99) reduced by ~9% during the busiest periods.
- For short_prompts: clock and sLRU both performed similarly; overhead of complex policy not justified given low reuse. CPU overhead of sLRU higher (~6% of CPU budget) in high-QPS short_prompts, so clock is preferred for short-heavy workloads.

Paging behavior and memory bandwidth sensitivity:
- Paging strategy: eager writeback-on-eviction vs deferred/async writeback. Eager writeback reduces host memory pressure but increases synchronous latency at eviction time.
- Measured host_device_bw per workload: in mixed-burst tests paging generates sustained 12-18GB/s traffic on A100-80GB, peaks up to 28GB/s on H100.
- Device memory bandwidth (on-chip) measured during KV read/write kernels is often the bottleneck for large KV lookups, not just PCIe. For quantized model runs, device memory throughput from cache read dominates compute when sequences are long because compute cost per token is reduced by quantization.
- Observed that when device memory bandwidth > 600 GB/s (H100), we still see memcpy/device-device overheads from scatter/gather patterns; suboptimal layout of KV storage causes many small device->device copies that reduce effective throughput by ~12%.

Hotspots and implementation notes:
- Current KV layout: per-token contiguous arrays interleaved across heads causing non-coalesced loads for some kernels. Reordering KV storage to head-major contiguous blocks yields ~7% improvement in device kernel bandwidth utilization in microbenchmarks.
- memcpy behavior: frequent small host<->device transfers degrade PCIe NVLink efficiency. Using batched page-in with pinned staging buffers reduces transfer overhead and improved effective BW by ~22% in the short_prompts workload.
- CPU-side locks: eviction bookkeeping serialized under a global lock in the current prototype. This causes visible CPU-side tail latency when eviction churn is high. Switching to sharded locks per cache partition reduces CPU stall time and lowers P99 by ~6%.

Quantitative results (representative):
- chat_multi_turn (A100-80GB):
  * baseline (LRU, eager writeback): reuse_rate 72%, throughput 1100 tokens/s, P95 42ms, P99 120ms, host_device_bw avg 6 GB/s bursts 14 GB/s.
  * sLRU + pinned batching + head-major layout: reuse_rate 76%, throughput 1290 tokens/s (+17%), P95 38ms (-9%), P99 102ms (-15%).
- short_prompts (A100-80GB):
  * baseline: reuse_rate 18%, evictions_per_minute 2200, throughput 5200 tokens/s, P99 spikes to 360ms during eviction storms.
  * clock + deferred async writeback + pinned staging: reuse_rate 20%, evictions_per_minute 1800, throughput 5600 tokens/s (+7.7%), P99 reduced to 210ms. CPU overhead down by ~4%.
- long_context (A100-40GB):
  * baseline: forced paging, throughput 600 tokens/s, device->host BW saturating at ~22 GB/s.
  * reduced kv-entry footprint via quantization + selective eviction: throughput 840 tokens/s (+40%), host_device_bw reduced to 14GB/s.

Operational implications and recommendations:
1) Adaptive eviction policy: use workload-class heuristics to pick policy. Default to segmented LRU for chat/multi-turn workloads; use clock for short-query heavy customers to reduce CPU overhead. Add ability to auto-switch based on observed reuse_rate and eviction churn.
2) Pinned staging buffers + batched page-ins: implement pinned host staging pool and coalesce page-in traffic to amortize PCIe/NVLink overheads. This reduces per-eviction synchronous latency and increases effective BW.
3) KV layout change: adopt head-major contiguous layout option derived from microbenchmarks to improve coalesced device memory access. Provide a compatibility flag to roll out incrementally.
4) Sharded eviction bookkeeping: remove global lock; shard by cache partition or model shard to reduce CPU stalls.
5) Telemetry: expose reuse_rate, evictions_per_minute, host_device_bw, and avg page-in size per-interval in console metrics so operators can detect eviction storms and tune cache size or policy.
6) Memory-pressure autoscaling: when host<->device BW approaches threshold for the instance type (e.g., sustained > 12GB/s on A100-80GB), trigger autoscale/burst or route new sessions to a lower-memory variant until pressure subsides.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Implement pinned staging pool and measure end-to-end improvement in production canary. (Action: Ravi to prototype, due 2026-03-29).
- Add auto-policy switcher based on realtime reuse_rate thresholds. (Action: Lin to design API and config knobs, due 2026-04-05).
- Add KV layout toggle and benchmark on cluster of H100 nodes; verify device-device bandwidth improvements at scale. (Action: Marcus to run cluster tests, due 2026-04-09).
- Expand profiling to additional model families (decoder-only 70B, encoder-decoder) to validate generality.

Open questions / risks:
- Quantization helps reduce KV size substantially, but changes to layout and kernel code may impact numerical parity; need evals for quality regression.
- Autoscaling decisions based on bandwidth require robust accurate measurement of host_device_bw in noisy multi-tenant environments. Need to validate signal quality.
- Some customers with strict determinism may prefer no eviction; need offering guidance / SLAs for pinned-resident KV and reserved GPU capacity.

Appendix: quick definitions and formulas used:
- reuse_rate = (sum over requests reused_kv_tokens) / (sum over requests total_kv_tokens_requested)
- eviction_churn = evictions_per_minute per device reported by runtime counters
- page-in size = bytes transferred host->device when a miss or eviction triggers a materialize

Notes to self / TODOs in doc:

- Add cost estimate for pinned staging memory vs expected reduction in cloud egress.
- Coordinate with product-owner to add reuse_rate KPI to the console (metric name: kvcache.reuse_rate).

End of note.
